passage: The news reached the kasba branch of the cooperative bank before lunch: Ramesh, who had joined on the same day as Jatin, was now assistant branch officer. Jatin smiled and shook his hand, then sat at his counter with his jaw clenched. Ramesh would now sign his leave forms. On the bus home, past the sugarcane fields, Jatin caught the thought going round and round: why him, why not me? He made himself stop. What did he actually have? A steady job four kilometres from his parents, a wife who laughed at his jokes, a scooter fully paid off. What could he control? The officer exam in June, and asking the manager what Ramesh had done that he hadn't. Three years ago he had been jobless, filling in forms at the cyber cafe. By the time he got home, he still wanted the post. He just wasn't angry about it.

qa.q: What post did Ramesh get?
qa.a: Assistant branch officer.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling at his counter after shaking Ramesh's hand?
qa.a: Under the smile he felt envious and resentful, his jaw clenched at the thought of Ramesh signing his leave forms.

qa.q: What questions did Jatin ask himself on the bus, and how did they help?
qa.a: What he actually has and what he can control, plus remembering being jobless three years ago, which let him keep wanting the post without the anger.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel if Jatin had stayed resentful?
qa.a: Ramesh might sense coldness from someone he joined with, making the new role lonelier.

passage: When the email went round the Toronto design studio announcing that Rania was now senior designer, Kwame felt his face go hot. They'd started the same month. He had stayed later, he told himself. He walked out for coffee to stop himself typing anything. In the queue he did what his older sister always told him: ask three questions. What do I have? A job I like, a portfolio twice as strong as last year's, a mentor who answers my messages. What can I control? My next project, and asking my lead exactly what senior means here. Where was I two years ago? Driving deliveries and sketching on my breaks. By the time his coffee came, the heat had gone. He went back in, stopped at Rania's desk and said, "Congratulations. Can you show me how you pitched the museum brief?"

passage:
Dear Baljeet Paaji,

You asked in your last letter how the new job is going. Honestly, last Monday I almost wrote to you in a rage. Arun, who joined the kitchen a month after me, was made sous chef. I spent the whole dinner service slamming pans.

Then I remembered what you told me when I was washing dishes at your dhaba: "Count what's in your hands before you count what's in someone else's." So I did. I have a job in a proper hotel kitchen. The head chef trusts me with the tandoor. I've learned three new sauces this year. What can I control? My knife speed, which is still slow, and asking chef what Arun did that I didn't. And four years ago I couldn't make a round roti.

I still want that sous chef coat. I'm just not angry about it any more.

With respect,
Lokesh

qa.q: Who was made sous chef?
qa.a: Arun, who joined the kitchen a month after Lokesh, was made sous chef.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel on the Monday Arun was promoted?
qa.a: Lokesh was furious and envious, so angry that the whole dinner service went in slamming pans.

qa.q: What helped Lokesh turn that anger into something useful?
qa.a: Remembering Baljeet's advice, Lokesh counted what was in hand, named what could be controlled and looked back four years, keeping the goal without the anger.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet would likely feel proud that Lokesh remembered the advice from the dhaba days and used it to handle a hard moment.

passage: Anirban, you asked on the phone why I sounded so off last month. Okay, honest version. I'm Ganga, twenty-five, and when my batchmate Swati got promoted to team lead, I was furious. Not at her, exactly. At the universe. I kept scrolling her post, all the congratulations. I couldn't sleep. Then one night I made myself do something my old teacher taught me: write what I actually have. A job I mostly like. A flat I pay for myself. My mother's health better this year. Then, what I can control: I can ask my manager what I'd need for the next step. And then I compared myself with me, two years ago, jobless and scared. That Ganga would be shocked by this one. I still want to lead a team someday. I just don't want Swati's news to decide my mood for a month.

passage: I sit across from Lakshmi at the insurance office in Chennai, so I saw the whole thing. When Kavin from our batch got the regional role, Lakshmi went very quiet. For two days she typed hard, skipped lunch, and gave one-word answers. I assumed she was angry; I can't be sure. On the third day, I saw her writing in a small notebook during tea. Later she told me, a bit embarrassed, that she'd written a list: what she had, what she'd learnt this year, what was in her hands. She also went and asked our manager what skills she needed for the next role. After that she laughed at lunch again. She congratulated Kavin, and it sounded real. I don't know what went on inside her. But she seemed to have found her own measuring stick, instead of Kavin's.

Lalremsiami, you're upset your batchmate got promoted first? Let me tell you what happened to me. I'm Jeevan, your Pu, your grandfather, and at twenty-five I was a junior clerk in Aizawl.
My friend from college was made section head before me. I was so angry I couldn't eat my lunch for a week. I kept counting what he had: a new office, a scooter.
One evening I sat down with a notebook. I wrote what I had: a steady job, a mother who was healthy, time to learn typing. And what I could control: my typing, my reports.
Two years later I was faster than anyone in the office. He still got promoted first. I stopped minding.

Kashish felt her jaw tighten. Two years, same projects. Why Uma?

passage:
Career coach's note, session 4.
Madhuri, 25, arrived frustrated. Her colleague Ramesh, who started the same week, was promoted to senior accountant on Monday, and she has been 'fuming for three days'. She described checking his desk, comparing hours and replaying their appraisal meetings. I didn't argue with the feeling. Instead I asked her to list what she actually has, what she can control and where she was two years ago. Her list surprised her: a steady job she likes, a qualification finished last year while working, and a manager who asks her opinion. Two years ago she was failing her exams. Her control list was short and clear: ask her manager for a development plan, and take the audit project she had been avoiding. She left calmer. She is still ambitious, and I told her that is a good thing. Review in a month.

qa.q: How had Madhuri been feeling since Ramesh's promotion?
qa.a: Madhuri had been frustrated and envious, fuming for three days and replaying their appraisals.

qa.q: Why was asking about her own past a useful step?
qa.a: It showed how far she had come, from failing exams two years ago to a qualification and a trusting manager now, which softens envy.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel if he knew about Madhuri's frustration?
qa.a: Ramesh might feel awkward or uneasy, since they started together and he may not know she is comparing.

Wednesday, late.
Sarika got the team lead role today. I clapped in the meeting, then went to the washroom and stood there fuming, fists tight. We joined on the same day. She's good, but I'm good too.
On the bus home I did the thing my old coach taught me: two lists.
What I actually have: a job I mostly like, a client who asks for me by name, my own rent paid, Ma's voice every Sunday.
What I can control: asking my manager what the lead role needs, finishing the analytics course, speaking up in reviews.
Then I looked back. Two years ago I cried after my first presentation. Today I ran one without notes.
I still want to lead a team. I just don't want envy choosing my mood.
Tomorrow I'll congratulate Sarika properly. Pallavi, you can want more and still be glad for her.

qa.a: The team lead role.
